idea: Hogarth's engraving The Distrest Poet (1741): a poet in a freezing garret, his wife darning, the milkmaid at the door with an unpaid bill, a map of 'the Gold Mines of Peru' on the wall. One added line underneath: 'Currently working on: Poverty, a Poem.' That is the real title on his desk, so it works as a dry joke about writing for a living that happens to be true.

Arcimboldo's The Librarian (c. 1566), the man built entirely out of books, redrawn as a single-ink line engraving, captioned 'Assembled from the collection.' It's a 450-year-old portrait of a reader who is literally what he reads, and an elegant badge for anyone who has run out of shelf space.

The 'Of Useless Books' woodcut that opens Sebastian Brant's Ship of Fools (Basel, 1494): a spectacled scholar flicking flies off a desk heaped with books he never reads. Caption: 'Fool no. 1: owns the books.' Brant put the book-collector first among all his fools, so this is a 15th-century diagnosis of the to-be-read pile.

Agostino Ramelli's book wheel from his 1588 machine book, a rotating reading desk that keeps a dozen open volumes on paddles like a waterwheel, captioned 'Too many tabs open, 1588.' It's a real Renaissance invention for reading several books at once, and it makes the case that browser tabs are an old idea.

Andrea Alciato's emblem from the first emblem book (Emblematum liber, 1531): a man whose one hand has wings and the other is chained to a heavy stone. Caption: 'Wings: talent. Rock: rent.' Alciato's motto says poverty keeps the greatest talents from rising, and the update makes that 500-year-old point land straight away for any struggling artist.

Rowlandson's etching of a skinny author holding out his manuscript to a fat, seated bookseller (1784), captioned 'Pitch meeting.' Nothing about the power dynamic of publishing has changed since, and writers will get it in a second.

The bookplate Dürer cut for his friend Willibald Pirckheimer, with its real motto 'SIBI ET AMICIS' and a small added line: 'For me and my friends. Bring it back.' Pirckheimer's library was among the finest in Germany, and the plate's generous motto plus one practical aside is the oldest argument about lending books.

Blake's relief-etched plate of 'The Tyger' from Songs of Experience (1794), with the caption 'Self-published. Wrote it, drew it, etched it, printed it.' Blake did all of that himself in his own workshop, so this is a classic poem that doubles as a badge for independent makers and zine-makers.

The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang, the oldest dated printed book (868), showing the Buddha preaching, with its colophon translated beneath: 'For universal free distribution.' Wang Jie paid for it to be printed for exactly that reason on behalf of his parents, so the world's first dated printed book was open access.

The squiggly plot diagrams Laurence Sterne printed in Tristram Shandy (Vol. VI, 1762) to show how each volume's story had wandered, captioned 'My plot, as drawn by the author.' They are real lines from a real novel, and they look like a modern doodle about how life never runs straight.

George Herbert's poem 'Easter Wings' (1633), set as in the first edition where the lines narrow and widen into two pairs of wings and are printed sideways on the page, captioned 'Shape poem. Tilt your head.' It's one of the earliest English concrete poems, beautiful as pure typography and a small puzzle to read.

The elephant carrying an obelisk woodcut from the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (Venice, 1499), set beside a tiny line drawing of Bernini's elephant obelisk in Rome's Piazza della Minerva (1667), captioned 'Rome built this from a book.' Bernini's monument really was inspired by that woodcut, which makes it a shirt about how books end up shaping cities.

An 18th-century illustration of Swift's Battle of the Books (1704), where the volumes in the King's Library go to war, centred on the bee and the spider. Caption: '"Sweetness and light." First said by a bee, in a fight between library books.' The phrase really does come from Swift's bee, and the reframing turns a famous cliché into a piece of literary trivia.

Étienne-Louis Boullée's 1785 design for the Royal Library in Paris, a vast barrel-vaulted hall lined with stepped terraces of books that was never built, captioned 'Unbuilt, 1785. Still the library everyone dreams of.' It's one of the most famous drawings in architecture, and it's a love letter to reading on a heroic scale.

Rembrandt's etching Saint Jerome Reading in an Italian Landscape (c. 1653), the saint lost in his book while his lion keeps watch, captioned 'Do not disturb. Translating.' Jerome translated the Bible into Latin and is the patron saint of translators (International Translation Day falls on his feast day, 30 September), so this one is for the people who carry meaning between languages.

Thomas Bewick's wood engraving of his own thumbprint with the words 'Thomas Bewick his mark', captioned only 'Signed.' Bewick, the master of English wood engraving, really did engrave his fingerprint as a signature tailpiece, and it's a quiet, clever image about authorship and craft.

One of the construction plates for the Romain du Roi, the typeface Louis XIV's commission designed in the 1690s on a fine grid of 2,304 small squares, with the capital 'R' plotted in compass arcs. Caption: 'Typeface designed by committee, 1695.' It looks like a blueprint and is a sly joke for designers who have sat through a review meeting.

Geofroy Tory's plate from Champ Fleury (1529) showing a Roman capital laid over a drawing of a human figure to fix its proportions, captioned 'Every letter has a body.' Tory really did argue that letterforms should follow the human frame, so it's a Renaissance anatomy lesson for type lovers.

Hogarth's The Bad Taste of the Town (1724), cropped to the woman pushing a wheelbarrow of Shakespeare, Jonson, Dryden and Congreve labelled 'Waste paper for shops', captioned 'Remaindered.' Hogarth was mocking a public that chose masquerades over literature, and the one-word update makes it a pointed shirt for anyone who works in books.

Holbein's woodcut portrait of Erasmus with his hand resting on the bust of Terminus, with a line adapted from his 1500 letter: 'When I get money, first Greek books, then clothes.' Erasmus really did put books ahead of clothes, and it's a scholarly, slightly self-mocking shirt for any reader whose budget goes the same way.
